A research paper, explained for everyone

Edit AI images with angle dials: each change is an arrow that can be reversed, blended and kept in its own spot

SphereEdit is a training-free add-on for Stable Diffusion that turns words like 'old', 'glasses' or 'lipstick' into same-length directions, mixes them with angles, and uses the model's attention to keep each edit where it belongs.

Based on the paper: SphereEdit: Spherical Semantic Editing in Diffusion Models · Salamata Konate, Hassan Hamidi, Elham Dolatabadi, Frank Rudzicz, Laleh Seyyed-Kalantri · WACV (IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision), Open Access version

🧒 In kid words

Ask a computer to add lipstick to a photo and it often changes the whole face. This trick changes only the lips, and lets you turn a dial to mix changes.

📖 The short version

AI image editors often change more than you asked: add lipstick and the skin tone shifts too. SphereEdit works out what each word changes, turns that into an arrow you steer with an angle, and uses a map of where the model 'looks' for each word to keep every edit in its own spot. It works with an existing AI image model as it is, with no extra training.

🔬 For experts

At each DDIM step of Stable Diffusion v1.5, SphereEdit takes the difference between the attribute-conditioned and null-text noise predictions, normalizes it to a unit direction, and restricts it with a token-specific cross-attention mask. Where two masks overlap, the directions are orthogonalized only there (masked Gram-Schmidt). The directions are mixed with spherical-coordinate weights (cos θ, sin θ cos φ, sin θ sin φ) and added to the base prediction. On two compositional face edits over 100 FFHQ images, it is best on 6 of 8 Table 1 scores against SEGA, Composable Diffusion, Cycle-Diffusion and TurboEdit (single seed, no variance reported).

Why it matters: The paper points to creative design, virtual try-on and content creation, where an edit must keep the person recognizable and change only what was asked. SphereEdit aims for that without fine-tuning or slow per-photo optimization, and its angle controls make the edits easy to reason about: reverse, blend or balance attributes.

0.7573 CLIP-I on Glasses+Mustache: how similar the edited photo stays to the original (higher is better; best of 5 methods, SEGA next at 0.7395) (source: Table 1)
0.7026 DINO on Glasses+Mustache: how well shape and layout are kept (higher is better; SEGA next at 0.6271) (source: Table 1)

Why does “add lipstick” change the whole face?

In one sentence: AI photo editors often change things you never asked for; SphereEdit treats each edit as an arrow (what changes) plus a place (where it may change).

Many image generators are diffusion models: they remove noise step by step, guided by text. To edit a photo, you change the text, say by adding “lipstick”.

Adding lipstick should not change skin tone, nor glasses reshape the face. Yet existing tools often leak: in the paper's comparison (Fig. 3, in Does it beat other editors?), two of four rival editors shift the whole photo's colour and change the face.

Toy example

Try it: one request, two ways to apply it

Click the buttons to switch how “add lipstick” is applied.

→

What to notice: same request both times. Unless it is told where it may act, the lipstick edit also repaints skin, cheeks and eyes.

Why? The paper's diagnosis: existing tools either push the whole picture one way or tie the edit to the right words, rarely both. They know what to change, not where.

SphereEdit's answer has two parts: an arrow for each edit that you can steer with a dial (next section), and a stencil (mask) cut from the model's own attention that keeps it in place (the section after). It is training-free: the existing model is used exactly as it is.

🧒 Explain it like I'm 8

It's a bit like a joystick plus a stencil. Push the stick toward “old” and the face ages; pull it back and it gets younger. A stencil is a sheet with a lip-shaped hole: spray paint, and only the lips get colored.

An edit is an arrow you can steer with an angle

In one sentence: One angle mixes two same-length edit arrows, so a single dial can add, reverse or blend edits while the weights stay balanced (their squares always add up to 1), which the paper uses to avoid over-saturation.

For each attribute, SphereEdit finds an arrow that adds it, freshly at every clean-up step (the next section shows how). The dial only sets how much of each arrow to use. Each arrow is rescaled into a unit vector so none drowns out another; a separate scale factor (usually 0 to 1) sets how strong an edit looks Sec. 3.2.

The angle θ gives each arrow a weight \(\lambda\): simply how much of that edit you apply. Old gets cos θ, Smiling gets sin θ: the dot’s shadows on the two axes below Fig. 1.

↩️ Reverse and blend

The paper reports this flip on real faces, given only “old” Sec. 4.2, and natural blends between Fig. 1. It calls the flip antipodal symmetry, though “old” is only approximately minus “young”.

🛡️ Bounded

cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, so turning the dial moves weight from one edit to the other; two separate sliders could both sit at full. If the arrows point at right angles (the paper assumes they roughly do), the total push stays at 1, versus about 1.41× for two full sliders. That is the paper’s “stable” goal Sec. 3. Single edits can still be turned up on purpose (Fig. 4 uses 7.5).

🔬 Go deeper: three edits need two angles (Eqs. 4–5)

For three attributes the circle becomes a sphere, and the weights are the standard spherical-to-Cartesian coordinates Eq. 4:

\[ \lambda_1=\cos\theta,\qquad \lambda_2=\sin\theta\cos\phi,\qquad \lambda_3=\sin\theta\sin\phi \] \[ \hat{v}^{Tr}_k=\lambda_k\,\hat{v}_k,\qquad \Delta\epsilon_t=\sum_{k:\,m_k(t)=1}\hat{v}^{Tr}_k \]
\(\hat{v}_k\)
unit direction of attribute \(a_k\), \(\hat v_k = v_k/\lVert v_k\rVert_2\)
\(\theta,\phi\)
the two angles that share the weight among three attributes
\(m_k(t)\)
1 if attribute \(k\) is switched on at denoising step \(t\)

With one attribute this reduces to a line (\(\theta=0\)), with two to the circle above (\(0\le\theta\lt 2\pi\)), with three to the full sphere (Eqs. 5, 8). Each direction can also be scaled by a factor between 0 and 1 to adjust how visible its edit is; single-attribute edits may use a larger factor (Fig. 4 uses scales of −7.5 and +7.5).

Note: the paper’s default \(\theta=\phi=\pi/2\) Sec. 4.1 is described as activating all attributes, but by Eq. 4 it gives weights \((0, 0, 1)\). The paper does not explain how the angles map to weights in its experiments. Try the “Paper default” preset below.

Toy example

Try it: two angles, three edits

Move θ and φ. The three weights always have squares that add up to 1.

What to notice: near θ = 55°, φ = 45° all three weights are about 0.58, an even three-way mix. At 90°, 90° only glasses is on. (Our toy only draws glasses when \(\lambda_3 > 0\).)

🔬 Go deeper: how solid are the “sphere” and the “opposite”?

The sphere. Normalizing puts every \(\hat v_k\) on the unit sphere; the angles only choose weights. The paper motivates this with prior studies indicating that diffusion latents are approximately spherical [9, 13], and an analogous finding for variational autoencoders [36] Sec. 3.2. It builds on that view rather than proving it.

The bound. \(\lVert\sum_k\lambda_k\hat v_k\rVert^2 = \sum_k\lambda_k^2 + 2\sum_{j\lt k}\lambda_j\lambda_k\langle\hat v_j,\hat v_k\rangle = 1 + \text{cross terms}\). It equals 1 exactly when the directions are orthogonal; the abstract credits approximate orthogonality for clean composition, and the next section shows how overlaps are handled. In any case the norm is at most \(\sum_k|\lambda_k|\le\sqrt{K}\).

The opposite. “Old ≈ −young” is observed (Fig. 1, Fig. 4), not derived.

Inside one step: find the arrow, find the place, untangle, add

In one sentence: At every clean-up step, SphereEdit asks the model, per edit, “what would this word change?” and “where?”, then adds the masked answer to its noise guess.

Stable Diffusion v1.5 cleans a picture in 50 steps; a real photo is first run backwards into noise (DDIM inversion). At each step the model's UNet guesses the noise to remove; SphereEdit changes only that guess.

  1. 1
    Find the arrow. Ask the model for its noise guess twice: once with the word “glasses”, once with no words at all. Whatever differs is what the word added; scaled to length 1, that is the arrow.
  2. 2
    Find the place. Cross-attention shows where the model looks for each word (glasses: eyes; beard: lower face). Its strongest spots become the stencil (mask).
  3. 3
    Untangle. Where two stencils overlap (mouth and beard), one arrow is adjusted: it drops the part it shares with the other, only there.
  4. 4
    Mix. Weight the arrows with the dial from above and add them.
  5. 5
    Add and step. Add the mix to the plain noise guess, each arrow acting only inside its stencil (the paper doesn't print exactly where the mask multiplies in Eq. 8).
Toy example

Try it: how big should the stencils be?

Drag the slider to resize the stencils; the buttons show the made-up attention maps.

What to notice: too wide, lipstick tints the cheeks; too tight, the glasses break up. The paper's real maps agree: glasses attention is sharp, lipstick's weaker and more diffuse, so lipstick is the threshold-sensitive one Fig. 5.

🔬 Go deeper: the equations of one step (Algorithm 1)

Latent diffusion: \(z_0 = \mathcal{E}(x_0)\), \(z_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,z_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon\) (Eq. 1); the UNet predicts \(\hat\epsilon = \epsilon_\theta(z_t, t, c)\) (Eq. 2). Trajectories \(\{z_t\}\) come from DDIM inversion; the decoder is used only to visualize.

\[ \mathbf{v}_k(t) = \epsilon_\theta(z_t,t,c_k) - \epsilon_\theta(z_t,t,c_\varnothing), \qquad \hat{\mathbf{v}}_k = \mathbf{v}_k / \lVert \mathbf{v}_k \rVert_2 \]
\(c_k,\ c_\varnothing\)
text embedding of attribute \(a_k\), and of the null (empty) text

The paper describes this as a local linearization of the denoiser in text-conditioning space (Eq. 3). Region \(\mathcal{R}_k(t)\) is the heatmap \(M_k(x,y,t)\) thresholded at quantile \(q\); the overlap mask is \(S_{jk} = \mathbf{1}[(x,y)\in\mathcal{R}_j\cap\mathcal{R}_k]\) (Eq. 6), and a masked Gram–Schmidt step decorrelates only there:

\[ \mathbf{v}_k \leftarrow \mathbf{v}_k - \langle \mathbf{v}_k, \mathbf{v}_j \rangle_{S_{jk}}\,(\mathbf{v}_j \odot S_{jk}) \]

Then \(\Delta\epsilon_t = \sum_{k:\,m_k(t)=1} \lambda_k \hat{\mathbf{v}}_k\) (Eqs. 5, 8) and \(\hat\epsilon(t) = \epsilon_{\text{base}}(t) + \Delta\epsilon_t\) replaces the denoiser output in the DDIM update (Eq. 9). Here \(m_k(t)\in\{0,1\}\) is the per-step on/off schedule (e.g. glasses only at later steps, after the face's structure forms) and \(\epsilon_{\text{base}} = \epsilon_\theta(z_t,t,c_\varnothing)\) (Algorithm 1, line 1). Cost: one extra UNet pass per active attribute per step.

Details the paper leaves open: how heads and layers are aggregated into \(M_k\) (Fig. 2 says “aggregation per-token, per-head/layer”); how the mask enters the final sum, since Eq. 8 does not show it explicitly; and whether \(\hat{\mathbf{v}}_k\) is re-normalized after the projection. Eq. 7 has no division by \(\lVert \mathbf{v}_j \odot S_{jk}\rVert^2\), so it is an exact projection only if \(\mathbf{v}_j\) is unit-norm on \(S_{jk}\). The paper doesn't say which attribute of a pair is projected, or in what order.

Settings Sec. 4.1, 4.4: Stable Diffusion v1.5, 50 steps, \(q = 0.8\) unless stated, seed 0, per-attribute start/end timesteps chosen per task. The Fig. 5 caption says \(q = 0\) means an empty mask and \(q = 1\) means no mask (which matches its images); the main text describes the low-\(q\) and high-\(q\) ends the other way round. The authors conclude that \(q = 0.8\) “offers the best compromise between edit strength and spatial precision.” This page follows the caption. Because the direction of \(q\) is ambiguous, the toy uses a plain “stencil size” percentage, which is not \(q\).

Does it beat other editors?

In one sentence: SphereEdit came first on 6 of the 8 reported scores and second on the other 2, on two face-edit tests over 100 photos, with one run and no spread reported (see the next section).

The authors compared SphereEdit with four existing editors (inversion-based, attention-manipulation and latent-direction methods): SEGA, Composable Diffusion, Cycle-Diffusion and TurboEdit. Scores are averaged over 100 face photos from FFHQ.

The scores cover two combined edits, Glasses + Mustache and Eyebrow + Lipstick:

  • CLIP-T ↑ higher is better: does the picture match the requested words?
  • CLIP-I ↑ higher is better: how similar the edited picture is to the original, according to CLIP (the paper uses it for identity).
  • DINO ↑ higher is better: similarity judged by another AI that is sensitive to shape and layout.
  • LPIPS ↓ lower is better: how visibly different the edit looks.

🔬 Go deeper: the four rivals, and how to read the scores together

The rivals, as the paper's related work describes them: TurboEdit uses accelerated inversion; Cycle-Diffusion relies on cycle-consistency; SEGA adds semantic guidance terms during sampling; Composable Diffusion combines concepts with energy-based models.

CLIP-T is the only score that rewards doing the edit; CLIP-I, DINO and LPIPS reward not changing the image. An editor that changed nothing would get perfect preservation scores and a poor CLIP-T, so the preservation scores only mean something alongside CLIP-T. SphereEdit's CLIP-T is first on one task and second on the other, so, at least by this measure, its preservation lead is not simply a result of doing less editing.

All CLIP-T values lie between 0.2203 and 0.2369. The paper reports one average per cell with no spread, so it is hard to tell whether gaps this small are meaningful (more in the next section). The paper does not spell out how each score is computed beyond citing the metrics.

What it can't promise yet

In one sentence: SphereEdit has only been tested on small mixes and a small benchmark, and its "reverse" direction does not always mean anything sensible.

Turn the dial from above to 180° and an edit flips: "minus old" means younger. Fig. 4 tests this flip on three attributes. In dial terms, −7.5 is the 180° direction (weight −1) with the strength turned up 7.5 times; the paper allows larger scales for single-attribute edits. Look at each row: what is the minus side supposed to be?

The authors raise exactly this: for attributes such as race, opposites are not well defined, and in medical imaging the "opposite" of a disease could be health or a different condition. They call it an open question for sensitive attributes.

Small mixes only. The paper tests up to three attributes. The formula extends to more, but the authors say its stability and interpretability there are unclear.

A small scoreboard. The previous section's numbers come from two face-edit pairs on 100 FFHQ images and one fixed random seed (seed 0), with one average per score and no spread, so tiny CLIP-T gaps are hard to judge.

Not instant. As in "Inside one step", the model is asked once more per attribute at every step; about 12 s for three attributes on an NVIDIA L40 graphics card Sec. 4.1.

Keep in mind: within these limits, the paper's evidence suggests cleaner face edits than the four editors tested. Read the dial's "reverse" side with care.

🔬 Go deeper: exactly what the evidence covers
  • One model: all experiments use Stable Diffusion v1.5 with 50 denoising steps and DDIM inversion of the input image.
  • Fixed settings: quantile threshold \(q = 0.8\) and \(\theta = \phi = \pi/2\) unless stated otherwise, which, by Eq. 4, would weight only the third attribute; see the note in the dial section. Each attribute's start and end timesteps are varied "depending on the task", and the paper does not list them per experiment.
  • Datasets: Table 1 uses 100 FFHQ images. The introduction also mentions CelebA-HQ, but no CelebA-HQ numbers are reported. Cars, pets and art appear only as example pictures (Fig. 1).
  • Antipodal symmetry is presented as approximate: "old" is approximately the negation of "young", observed in Fig. 1 and Fig. 4 rather than derived.

Glossary

Antipodal symmetry
The observation that pointing an attribute's arrow the opposite way gives roughly the opposite attribute, like old versus young.
Attribute direction
The difference between what the model predicts with an attribute's text (like 'glasses') and with empty text, used as an arrow pointing toward that attribute.
CLIP-T / CLIP-I
Scores from the CLIP model: CLIP-T checks how well the image matches the requested text, CLIP-I checks how much it still looks like the original subject.
Cross-attention map
A heat map showing which parts of the image the model connects to a given word in the text.
DDIM inversion
A way to run the denoising process backwards so a real photo can be turned into noise and then rebuilt, with edits along the way.
Denoiser (UNet)
The part of the diffusion model that guesses, at each step, which part of the current image is noise.
Diffusion model
An AI that makes images by starting from random noise and removing a little noise at a time until a picture appears.
DINO score
A similarity score from the DINO vision model used here to check that the image's structure and layout are kept.
FFHQ
A public collection of high-quality face photos widely used in image research; the paper scores 100 of them.
GPU (NVIDIA L40)
A graphics card, the kind of computer chip that runs AI models quickly; the paper times its edits on an NVIDIA L40.
LPIPS
A measure of how different two images look to a neural network; lower means fewer visual changes or artifacts.
Mask (stencil)
The yes/no region, cut from a word's attention map, where that word's edit is allowed to act.
Mask threshold q
The quantile cut-off used to turn an attention heat map into a yes/no region where an edit is allowed.
Noise prediction
The denoiser's guess of the noise at one step; SphereEdit edits this guess rather than the pixels.
Orthogonalization (Gram-Schmidt)
Removing the shared part of two arrows so they no longer push in the same direction; SphereEdit does this only where two edits overlap.
Spherical coefficients
Weights built from angles (cos and sin) that split a unit budget among the attribute arrows; a separate scale factor can then make each edit stronger or weaker.
Stable Diffusion v1.5
The publicly available text-to-image diffusion model all of the paper's experiments use.
Training-free
Works with an existing model as-is, with no fine-tuning or extra learning.
Unit vector
An arrow scaled to length 1, so only its direction matters.

How this page was made

This explainer was written by a team of AI agents. A lead editor read the paper and planned the page; experts wrote the sections: Diffusion-editing and cross-attention expert (Why does 'add lipstick' change the whole face?, Inside one step: find the arrow, find the place, untangle, add); Spherical-geometry and explorable-toy designer (An edit is an arrow you can steer with an angle); Image-editing evaluation and responsible-AI analyst (Does it beat other editors?, What it can't promise yet). The page was then revised over 1 round using feedback from simulated readers (Maya, 8, reading with her dad, Jordan, 15, a high-school student, Prof. Elena Rossi, 55, a professor in the field, Margaret, 70, a retired librarian), reviews by the experts of each other's sections, and a fact-checker that compared every section with the paper.

It can still contain mistakes: the original paper is the authoritative source. Anything marked Toy example is a simplified teaching illustration with made-up numbers, not a result from the paper. Figures marked From the paper are reproduced from it.
